sketches.title: Signs of the Times
sketches.premise: A real town name appears on the sign; invent the ridiculous local story that supposedly put it there. Both players answer, then the Host reveals the real, checkable origin and awards points for the best story that still fits the place name. Keep it plausible enough to make someone say, “Honestly, that tracks.”
sketches.criterion: The story must plausibly explain how the exact place name arose, while keeping the name’s key words recognizable and in the stated order.
sketches.move_shape: Write one two-sentence origin story for the sign, using both name words as concrete clues; e.g., for **Bacon, Indiana**: “A farmer found a slab of bacon nailed to his fence after a prank. The joke stuck, and so did the name.”

sketches.title: Name Game
sketches.premise: The Host gives you a real place name made from two ordinary words. Sell a believable reason those two words became a place name—without looking anything up. After both answers, the Host shares the real origin and gives points for the answer that feels most like a story locals would actually repeat.
sketches.criterion: The answer must make both ordinary words function as the two necessary parts of one plausible naming event, not merely mention them.
sketches.move_shape: Give one punchy sentence containing a specific naming moment; e.g., for **Blue Ball, Pennsylvania**: “A blue-painted ball hung outside the first tavern, warning travelers that the owner’s team never missed a game.”

sketches.title: Map Lies
sketches.premise: You are a charming liar explaining a real place name to a tourist. Invent the cleanest false origin you can, then hear the other player’s version before the Host reveals the boring—or wonderfully weird—truth. Points reward a lie that sounds locally authentic without becoming a damn fairy tale.
sketches.criterion: The answer must offer one coherent, believable origin for the exact place name and must not contradict the place’s basic geography or history supplied on the card.
sketches.move_shape: Write a one-sentence explanation a tour guide could say with a straight face; e.g., for **Dead Horse, Colorado**: “The trail ended at a horse-shaped rock where exhausted riders stopped to rest and leave offerings.”

sketches.title: Two-Word Town
sketches.premise: Every card is a real place whose name uses two everyday words. Turn those words into a tiny founding legend: who said them, why, and why everybody kept repeating them. The Host checks the real origin afterward and scores the legend for fit, snap, and shameless charm.
sketches.criterion: The answer must connect the two name words through a single memorable event in which both words could naturally have been spoken or recorded as the name.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence of dialogue or reported speech that could have created the name; e.g., for **Hell, Michigan**: “When asked where the muddy road led, a furious traveler shouted, ‘Go to hell!’ and the signmaker took him literally.”

sketches.title: Local Lore
sketches.premise: Make up the kind of origin story a town would print on a souvenir mug: specific, proud, and just suspiciously convenient. Both players get the same real place name, then the Host reveals the documented origin and rewards the story that best turns two plain words into local legend.
sketches.criterion: The answer must preserve the place name exactly and make its two words the central evidence of a plausible community origin, rather than decorative jokes.
sketches.move_shape: Write a two-sentence tourist-brochure blurb with one named object, person, or mistake; e.g., for **Truth or Consequences, New Mexico**: “A radio show offered the town a chance to rename itself for publicity. The locals chose the host’s slogan because apparently dignity had left town.”

sketches.title: Origin Story
sketches.premise: The Host deals a real place name and asks for the first version of its story—the one a tired settler, mapmaker, or smart-ass neighbor might have told. Answer with a plausible mini-origin, then compare it with the documented truth. The best answer travels farthest from the facts while still making the name feel inevitable.
sketches.criterion: The answer must explain the name as a believable result of an identifiable person’s action, mistake, description, or remark, with both name words doing real work.
sketches.move_shape: Write one vivid sentence naming the trigger and the person or group who spread it; e.g., for **Ding Dong, Texas**: “A roadside store hung a bell, and passing children named the stop after the sound before the owner could think of anything less stupid.”
